title: Unsecured Credentials: Credentials in Registry
summary: This sub-technique is credential collection from the Windows registry, which stores configuration for the operating system and for applications, including settings that hold passwords in readable form. Typical targets are autologon values, which retain a default logon name and password so a machine signs in without interaction, and application keys that cache service or database credentials. The access pattern is a broad keyword search rather than a targeted read, because the adversary does not know the exact key path in advance, so command-line registry queries that scan whole hives for terms such as password or the string value type are characteristic. The evidence therefore sits in process creation logging, including security event 4688 and Sysmon event 1, where the query tool and its arguments are recorded. Legitimate administration also queries the registry, so the discriminator is the sweep pattern, the account performing it, and whether the same session then authenticates elsewhere with the recovered value.

beginner.definition: Windows keeps a large settings store called the registry. Programs and the system save options there, and some of those options include passwords. This sub-technique is when an attacker searches the registry for saved passwords and then uses them.
beginner.whyItMatters: Some machines are set to sign in automatically, and that saved password sits in the registry. Reading it gives the attacker a working account without any guessing. The search is quick, quiet, and needs only an ordinary command on the machine.
howItWorks: Windows stores system and program settings in a database called the registry.
Some of those settings hold passwords, for example the values used for automatic sign-in.
An attacker runs a search command that scans the registry for the word password.
The command lists every matching setting, and that narrows the useful targets.
The attacker then reads the matching values, which include any saved credentials in clear form.
Those credentials are then used to log in to other machines or services.
beginner.example: Think of an office where each desk keeps a locked drawer. The label on every drawer says what is inside. A searcher walks along the row reading labels until one says spare keys. They open that drawer and take what they need. The drawers were never forced. The information was simply written where anyone could read it.
takeaways: Saved automatic sign-in passwords in the registry are a real risk.
Command-line logging records registry searches and their exact arguments.
A registry sweep by a normal user account deserves investigation.

objectives: Explain what the Windows registry stores and why credentials end up there.
Describe how an automatic sign-in value becomes a usable credential.
Explain why attackers search registry hives by keyword instead of exact path.
Identify the process creation records that capture registry query commands.
Describe how to reduce credentials stored in registry values.
